After NVIDIA’s Leadership Transition, Which AI Growth Expectations Need Reassessment?

From customer financing and GPU–ASIC procurement to HBM orders and hosting cash flows

17 November 2026 · Updated edition

Built on AlphaMap relationships and public disclosures

1. After NVIDIA’s leadership transition, CoreWeave’s expansion depends on funding execution2. The second hop requires customer concentration, alternative funding and lease timing3. ASICs supply roughly 75% of incremental desired devices; qualified capacity still constrains supply4. Earlier procurement can change annual HBM demand without changing installed capacity5. Identified configuration changes explain only 2.8% of HBM at constant device quantitiesInvestment view: identify underfunded expansion before forecasting downside transmissionModel and evidenceSources

Jensen Huang left NVIDIA’s CEO role on November 12. NVIDIA sells accelerators, purchases capacity from selected customers and provides specified credit support. The transition raises an investment question: which customer expansions can still be delivered on schedule, and where could changes in financing reach equipment orders and hosting revenue?[1][2][19]

Our base case is that existing contracts and operating capacity support near-term business continuity. The distant projects requiring reassessment are those that still lack sufficient financing and depend on additional NVIDIA support. A downgrade to procurement and commissioning forecasts through this financing channel requires reduced support and insufficient replacement funding before equipment payments. ASIC financing involving Broadcom, and projects supported by Google or AMD, require separate assessments under their own contracts.[2][11][39][49]

Following AlphaMap’s customer, supply and credit relationships reveals a material timing distinction: Core Scientific’s future contracted capacity is diversifying, while all of its current colocation revenue still comes from CoreWeave. HBM suppliers likewise need separate assessments of negotiated 2027 supply and absorption of new 2028 capacity. We calculate these company exposures and procurement conditions to identify which growth expectations already have delivery support and which still depend on financing closing.[7][20][42]

1. After NVIDIA’s leadership transition, CoreWeave’s expansion depends on funding execution

NVIDIA must purchase specified unsold residual CoreWeave capacity when delivery, service availability and other conditions are met. The agreement has an initial value of $6.3 bn and runs through April 2032. NVIDIA bears the obligation; it does not guarantee all CoreWeave debt. In announcing the transition, the board said it expected existing commitments and the product roadmap to continue. Future additions require separate assessment: NVIDIA’s guarantees for 4.25 GW at SB Energy generally become effective as the relevant leases commence and trigger payment on specified tenant defaults. NVIDIA retains discretion over additional support for a further 3.8 GW.[1][2][19]

CoreWeave’s first-nine-month operating cash flow of $5.638 bn covered 23.9% of cash investment in property, equipment and capitalised software; $21.346 bn of net financing had already occurred. Management separately expected $9 bn of prepayments and deposits over the following three months. If 20% arrived late and only $1 bn of otherwise unallocated replacement funding were available in that window, $0.8 bn would remain unreplaced. This measures cash-timing sensitivity; it is not an observed financing shortfall or revenue loss. Even if replacement loans cover the gap, higher interest can reduce cash available to equity without requiring a matching reduction in commissioning.[3][5]

The commissioning pace of new CoreWeave projects therefore depends on whether customer contracts can support financing and whether cash arrives before equipment payments. The residual-capacity agreement provides demand support. Additional loans, customer advances and future support determine when projects that remain underfunded can purchase equipment.

2. The second hop requires customer concentration, alternative funding and lease timing

Core Scientific, or CORZ, illustrates the distinction. Of CoreWeave’s 590 MW of leased capacity, 485 MW was billing, approximately 82%. AMD directly leases 377 MW; an unnamed Neocloud leases another 152 MW with conditional AMD credit support for those specified leases. CoreWeave represents approximately 53% of the roughly 1,120 MW in these two contracted IT-capacity groups.[6][49]

Diversification in future capacity has not yet become diversification in current revenue. At September-end, neither group of AMD-associated new leases had commenced. All CORZ colocation revenue came from CoreWeave, which represented approximately 84% of group revenue for the first nine months. Management expects delivery of the additional approximately 530 MW from 2027 through year-end 2028; construction still requires external financing. Existing collections, billing commencement on the remaining 105 MW and financing for new projects require separate forecasts. A 53% capacity share cannot be used to adjust all CORZ revenue. Rent credits and project debt service also separate billing from the timing of cash available to equity.[6][7][8]

A shared customer creates another transmission path. Microsoft buys services from CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, but IREN’s associated project loan is drawn in four tranches, subject to delivery milestones and conditions precedent. A funded customer budget does not establish immediately drawable operator cash. All three share customer-budget exposure; demand is deduplicated only when the same capacity or end workload appears at successive contract layers.[3][12][14]

Alternative funding also changes the assessment. Google’s credit support for specified Akela leases takes effect upon lease commencement and is triggered by specified defaults. Its choice between curing rent and assuming the leases or paying a termination amount affects continuity of remaining lease revenue. The $63 bn SPV transaction involving Broadcom has committed financing to buy XPU and networking equipment and lease it to Anthropic; Broadcom’s residual-value support corresponds to the first-lien debt portion. These arrangements predate the leadership transition. They do not demonstrate orders moving after the event, but they provide financing commitments from other counterparties for specified ASIC projects. NVIDIA’s share and total HBM demand therefore require tracking these customers’ purchases separately.[11][39]

How does the relationship view change the company assessment?

CORZ customer links require lease status: new counterparties represent nearly half of future contracted capacity, while current colocation revenue remains entirely with CoreWeave. Microsoft’s shared-customer links require each operator’s advance-payment and drawdown terms. AlphaMap supplies existing cross-company relationships; this study adds public-contract and financial verification to derive distinct revenue, funding and cash-flow judgments from the same industry event.[3][6][7][14][49]

3. ASICs supply roughly 75% of incremental desired devices; qualified capacity still constrains supply

We backcast the estimated 2026 high-end cloud accelerator base from a public industry summary, then specify independent forward growth and product mix. Desired 2028 procurement reaches approximately 30.11 m devices, with ASICs at about 60%. ASICs contribute roughly 75% of the increase from 2026. Assuming comparable GPU device cost is three times ASIC cost and prices remain unchanged, this path requires approximately 66% more equipment budget. It is a demand scenario, not a fully confirmed order book.[28]

AWS’s additional 2 m GPU plan provides a named demand anchor, although calendar-year phasing remains an assumption. The 5 GW Anthropic programme involving Google and Broadcom does not explain all TPU growth: under our phasing, other customers must still grow approximately 52% in 2027 and 61% in 2028.[29][48]

On supply, 8.16 m annual wafers of matched front- and back-end processing capacity, at about 960 nominal GB of qualified output per wafer, yield 7.8 EB of effective Top3 HBM capacity in 2028. Low and high engineering cases are 5.9 EB and 10.3 EB. Fab phasing, HBM allocation, die area and effective recovery are recorded separately; December monthly capacity is not multiplied by twelve.[25][26][27]

7.8 EB is a capacity forecast; revenue still depends on customer procurement. The full desired configuration of covered devices requires approximately 11.1 EB. Product generations, customer qualification, financing and delivery conditions limit realised purchases. Demand measures device-embedded HBM, while suppliers serve other customers and changes in raw-HBM and work-in-process inventory also affect shipments. Subtracting the two measures would not establish total-industry surplus.

4. Earlier procurement can change annual HBM demand without changing installed capacity

With 25% annual facility-IT growth, mid-case device power, identical opening inventory and a one-quarter physical commissioning lag, procurement one quarter versus four quarters ahead produces approximately 4.96 EB versus 7.31 EB of embedded HBM in 2028. Year-end installed AI-system IT capacity is 99.7 GW in both cases. The roughly 2.4 EB gap is conditional on exogenously specified procurement windows; it has not been identified as the effect of the leadership transition or financing contraction. Applying it to company forecasts requires identifying who can take delivery early.[36]

The model begins with 82 GW of global data-centre IT capacity in 2025 and separately calculates conventional servers, AI-equipment retirements and new commissioning. The 25% path is an accelerated-growth assumption: approximately 250 GW in 2030, above the IEA’s 174 GW forecast. Fast-growing regional samples cannot calibrate a global rate. We show 20%, 25% and 30% growth together with device-power and procurement-window sensitivities, without selecting a calibrated most-likely whole-industry path.[36][37]

At year-end 2028, uninstalled equipment equals 43.8 GW in the four-quarter case and 10.1 GW in the one-quarter case. Using assumed GPU and ASIC prices of $30,000 and $10,000, the longer window ties up approximately $217.4 bn more year-end accelerator capital, excluding other system components and financing costs. This scales inventory capital; it is not an observed financing gap. Separately, CoreWeave reclassified $1.9 bn from deferred revenue to customer liabilities in Q3 after the associated contracts became cancellable. Refundability affects whether advances can support long-term inventory purchases.[3]

5. Identified configuration changes explain only 2.8% of HBM at constant device quantities

Regular Rubin retains its disclosed 288 GB. We model the eligible Ultra 8-Hi engineering branch and the choice between MI450X at 288 GB/eight stacks and MI455X at 432 GB/twelve stacks. At the stated covered-product mix and adoption rates, HBM in the same desired 2028 devices falls from 11.42 EB to 11.10 EB: approximately 0.32 EB, or 2.8%. This configuration effect cannot directly refute a 30% revision over a different device universe.[31][32][33][34]

If 8-Hi pricing per bit is 10–20% above 12-Hi, HBM revenue per otherwise identical device still falls approximately 20–27%, requiring 25–36% more devices to offset it. This is a same-generation pricing sensitivity. AMD’s lower-stack-count alternative does not inherit that premium, and 2027 price expectations are not treated as 2028 transaction prices.[35]

Comparing the external research

The November 17 SemiAnalysis report is recorded separately from the earlier November 13/November 2 charts. The newer original, comparison baseline and power perimeter have not been obtained in verifiable form. No SemiAnalysis revision rate entered our supply-demand inputs. Current independent results support distinguishing company, funding and procurement conditions; they do not adjudicate the stated 17% cumulative silicon-area, 30% 2028 HBM and 34% 2030 power reductions. The 2.8% constant-device configuration effect and roughly 2.4 EB procurement-window gap each have defined scopes; neither is a whole-market revision.[16][18]

Investment view: identify underfunded expansion before forecasting downside transmission

We retain near-term delivery continuity supported by existing contracts and remain cautious on distant expansion without secured financing. For CoreWeave, the decisive observations are advance receipts and new loans. CORZ collections remain concentrated in CoreWeave, while financing and lease commencement for AMD-associated projects require separate estimates. We retain conditional milestone expectations by mid-2027 for APLD’s 150 MW and Akela’s 336 MW under construction; facility MW do not directly establish GPU shipments.[3][6][7][9][11]

Micron’s and Samsung’s negotiated 2027 supply provides a basis for near-term HBM delivery visibility. Returns on 2028 expansion still require verification of procurement funding and absorption of qualified capacity. Disclosed independent financing arrangements give some ASIC projects a basis to proceed; drawdowns and deliveries require separate verification. A change in NVIDIA’s share cannot be equated with the same change in industry-wide memory demand.[20][39][42]

Lowering procurement and commissioning forecasts because of a funding shortfall requires evidence of reduced drawable funding or delayed advances, together with insufficient replacement cash for equipment or construction payments. The relevant contracts then determine procurement delays, later commissioning and deferred hosting billing. Completed drawdowns, received advances and customer acceptance that starts billing can weaken that downside path. Equity prices can anticipate these developments; no validated short-return signal is claimed here.

LunarTulip Research examines how industry changes reach company cash flows through customers, contracts and capital expenditure. This study starts from AlphaMap relationships, adds verified public evidence and independent calculations, and brings financing support, shared customers and alternative procurement into the same investment assessment.
